lines.note: Taishoku is eating a great deal; the repeated headword begins the construction with the object particle. The gloss reads Muito, not the OCR's Maito.
Suru completes taishoku wo suru, explicitly translated as eating much. This is the continuation of the preceding example rather than an independent entry.
Taishoogun denotes the principal commander or general. The scan has one initial T, not the OCR's TFa-, and a caron over o.

runs.text: Taixu. Vôqini mamoru. i, Cunino nuxi.

lines.note: Taishu is explained through 'guard greatly' and kuni no nushi, the lord of a country. These Japanese explanatory equivalents remain roman, distinct from the Portuguese on the next row.

runs.text: Senhor grande de algum reino, ou mais.

lines.note: The Portuguese defines the lord as ruling one kingdom or more, completing the territorial sense of taishu rather than the drinking sense below.
This homograph taishu concerns heavy drinking, with oozake as its Japanese equivalent. The example is divided after Tai-; the italic Vt introduces it.
Tai-shu de gozaru describes being a heavy drinker. The Portuguese offers both being a wine drinker and drinking much, with the latter alternative continuing below.
Beber muito vinho completes the second rendering of the example. Vinho is the dictionary's Portuguese description of the alcoholic drink; it is not a Japanese word to mark separately.

Taishutsu is withdrawing or leaving, matching tornar-se or ir-se. The cramped Xrizoqi is retained as printed rather than silently expanded to expected shirizoki; the following izzuru supplies 'go out'.

runs.text: A noite antes da comendação que fazẽ

lines.note: Taiya is the night preceding a memorial observance for a deceased person. The relative clause continues onto the next two rows; the abbreviation tilde in fazẽ is retained.

runs.text: pello defunto, & do conuite que dão aos Bõ-

lines.note: The observance is for the deceased and includes a banquet for Buddhist clergy and others. Bõ- begins Portuguese bonzos, so its initial B belongs with the italic gloss, not a separate roman Japanese span.
Zos completes the divided word for Buddhist clergy, followed by 'and others'. The brief physical continuation remains separate and is not a new headword.

Taiyaku is an expensive, valuable medicine, clarified by takai kusuri. The abraded consonant in cuſuri is read as long s from its remaining trace and the medicine gloss, not preserved as the OCR's meaningless cuuri.
Completes preço, giving a medicine of value and good quality. Both this fragment and the hyphenated beginning belong to the Portuguese definition.
Taiyei, explained as ookina itonami, is a large undertaking or occupation. The example concerns costly enterprises rather than merely being personally busy.

runs.text: ou negocio, & de gaſto como de obras, con-

lines.note: The undertaking involves business and expenditure, with construction works and a banquet as examples. Con- is the beginning of convite on the next physical row.
Uite completes conuite, banquet, followed by the printed abbreviation for 'and so forth'. It closes the preceding entry without beginning a new one.
Taiyeki means great advantage or profit, corresponding to ookina toku. The final upright S. marks written usage; it is not part of the italic Portuguese definition.
Taiyoo and taiyoona describe equivalence or matching form. The printed y letters correct the OCR's Taijǒ and tajǒna; l introduces the alternative adjectival form.
The equivalence extends to quality and strength. Taiyoona begins the example describing equally matched opponents on the following line.
Aite completes taiyoona aite, rendered as equal competitors. This supports a sense of matching ability rather than numerical identity.
Taiyooni is the corresponding adverb; the dictionary supplies only the grammatical label Adu. here. No unattested definition is added to the short entry.
Taiyoo is now the philosophical pairing of substance and accident. Its circumflex contrasts with the preceding entry's caron, and the abbreviated q̃ continues the explanation below.

The definition distinguishes substantial from accidental or added properties. Two c types are visible in accidentari-, correcting the OCR's single c; the printed edge hyphen divides the adjective continued below.
As completes accidentarias, followed by postiças, properties added or imposed. The row closes the contrast between essential and incidental features.
Taiyuu is great bravery, matched by ookina isami and grande valentia. The scan shows the long-vowel mark in Vôqina that the OCR omitted.
Presteza adds readiness or alacrity to the bravery gloss. This short Portuguese continuation belongs to taiyuu and carries no new headword.
Taiza, with mukai za, describes sitting opposite or on the same level. The Portuguese continues from being on the same floor or level to facing one another.

runs.text: hum de fronte do outro no zaxiqui.

lines.note: The definition specifies one person facing another in a zashiki. Zaxiqui is a Japanese room term embedded in the Portuguese sentence and is flagged separately for optional typeface review.
Taizai denotes staying or detention; todokoori and imasu explain remaining in a place. The printed circumflex and comma are retained rather than normalizing the historical form.

Taizoku is presented as another name for the first month, shoogat(su). Pri- is wholly italic. The first o-mark is damaged and its baseline circumflex is retained provisionally; the later carons are clearer and are not imposed on that occurrence.
Meira completes primeira: the first lunar month or month of the year. The physical division is retained instead of joining the word across rows.

The Portuguese evidently intends a female Buddha named Dainichi. In ſemea the first type lacks a clear f crossbar, so the aligned long-s reading is retained with a caveat, not silently corrected to femea. Fotoque and the divided name occur within Portuguese exposition; the doctrinal description is the dictionary's own.
Nichi completes Dai-nichi from the preceding line. The scan supports nichi, not the OCR's ntchis; this very short continuation is part of the same name.
Taji is another temple, explained by ta no tera and Portuguese outra varela. The final i of the headword is visible and was omitted by OCR.
The next taji means another matter, ta no koto, rather than a temple. The example begins taji wo and continues with a negative verb on the next row.
Majiyenu completes the instruction not to mix in another matter. The Portuguese negative confirms the negative Japanese ending, not a positive injunction to combine things.
Tajit, explained by bet(su) no hi, means another day. The bare final t is the dictionary's checked-syllable notation and is not expanded in the transcription.

The separate homograph tajit means many days, with amata no hi as its Japanese explanation. The final worn type is t, not OCR e; the supplied NINJAL index independently lists both adjacent Tajit entries. Lexical aid: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, v202510, CC BY 4.0; the supplied scan remains authoritative for transcription.
Tajoo ippen describes wholehearted concentration, using all one's strength and care. The initial is T and the second word has two p types, correcting Fajǒ iopen.
The definition excludes attending to anything else. The following example repeats tajoo ippen; the abbreviated nasal mark over its final e is preserved before the printed division.

The example means studying with wholehearted application. Gacumonuo is read through considerable abrasion at the n and word junction; the study gloss supports gakumon wo rather than treating the OCR's gap as a separate word.

Diligencia and cuidado complete the description of diligent study. The word's middle is abraded, but its remaining types support diligencia, not dili gentia; a second wholehearted-action example starts after the paragraph mark.

The second example is desiring salvation or a favorable next existence with complete devotion. The faint object-particle u in goxǒuo corrects OCR r; the damaged long-vowel marks are retained conservatively.

runs.text: com todas a forças, penſametos, cuidado, &c.

lines.note: The Portuguese continues 'with all strength, thoughts, and care'. The abraded source is retained as a and penſametos rather than supplying an unseen plural s or nasal abbreviation; the final damaged sign is the usual ampersand in &c.
Tama is a precious stone. The worn example begins tama wo miga-, polishing a gem, with qu on the next physical line; no terminal hyphen is supplied where the print does not establish one.

Qu completes migaku, and the Portuguese describes working precious stones. The severely abraded Lauràr and pedras are usable contextual readings supported by remaining strokes; a new tama wo example continues at the top of column 2.
Tsuranuru completes tama wo tsuranuru across the column boundary. The Portuguese describes adorning or beautifying; Ornar replaces OCR Orntar without modernizing afermoſear.
The comparison is to someone threading precious stones. This completes the ornamenting example and explains the connection with the preceding gem entry.
Tama now denotes a projectile or ball. Qinno ta- begins kin no tama, whose anatomical application is made explicit in the next line; Qinno has no internal word space.
Ma completes tama in the phrase for testicles, which the Portuguese describes as their round bodies or 'grains'. The example is distinct from the precious-stone sense above.
Tamabauaqi is an elevated expression for a broom, explicitly described as a word praising a broom. The scan begins with T, not the OCR's F; the historical bauaqi spelling is not modernized.

runs.text: Vaßoura: às vezes ſe toma pollo ramo que eſtà

lines.note: The gloss gives a broom, then a branch used as a tavern sign. The printed ß-like double-s form in Vaßoura is retained instead of normalized to modern vassoura.

runs.text: às portas das tauernas à maneira de vaßoura.

lines.note: The branch stands at tavern doors in the shape of a broom. This explains the figurative association with drinking used in the following example.
Urei wo haroo tamabauaqi is a broom that sweeps away sorrow. The italic Vt introduces the Japanese example, and the Portuguese begins its broom-or-wine-branch interpretation.

runs.text: ramo de vinho que bota a tristeza fora.

lines.note: The wine branch drives sadness away. The Portuguese completes the figure of speech rather than defining a second physical tool.
Tamabito is a lapidary or person knowledgeable about gems. Lapidairo is the actual historical Portuguese form and is not replaced by modern lapidário.
Precioſas qualifies the stones in the lapidary definition. The one-word continuation remains its own physical line.
Tamaboko is marked as poetic and equated with michi, a road. The P. is upright in this impression, as are the Japanese equivalent and its introductory i.

runs.text: Tamacazzura. P. i, Vonnano yoi cami-

lines.note: Tamakazura is poetic language for a woman's beautiful hair. The Japanese equivalent ends here with cami-, and the upright P. marks the poetic register.
Gue completes camigue, hair, and the Portuguese gives a woman's beautiful head of hair. The divided Japanese form is not a separate entry.
Tamadare is a poetic equivalent of tamasudare. The Portuguese begins a description of rich or fine mats; P. is upright rather than italic.
Ras completes esteiras, followed by ricas. This finishes the material description of the fine blinds or mats, not a new headword.
Tamadasuki first names raising and securing the sleeves. The Portuguese verb for tying them begins with a- at the right edge and continues below.

runs.text: marralas de tras pera fazer algũa couſa liure-

lines.note: Marralas completes amarralas, tying the sleeves behind oneself to work freely. The scan has continuous marralas, not the OCR's mar alas; liure- continues on the next row.

runs.text: mente ſem ſe molhar, ou çujar. ¶ Item, O

lines.note: The tying allows work without getting wet or dirty. Item introduces a related concrete sense, the cord used to secure the sleeves.

runs.text: cordão, ou circulo com que ſe apanhão, & a-

lines.note: The second sense is the cord or loop with which the sleeves are gathered. The closing a- again begins a divided form of amarrar.
Marrão completes amarrão and specifies tying the sleeves behind the body. This finishes the second sense of tamadasuki.
Tamagari gives principal forms for being startled or astonished. Sed meli- begins the Latin editorial preference for a different form on the following row.
The printed ùs completes meliùs, 'better', recommending tamaguiru. The Latin editorial phrase is italic while the Japanese recommended form is roman.

runs.text: Hũa aruore que tem as fo-

lines.note: Tamagashiwa is marked poetic and described as a tree with beautiful leaves. The upright P. precedes the italic gloss; fo- begins folhas below.
Lhas completes folhas, describing the tree's leaves as very beautiful. The gloss does not by itself identify a modern botanical species.
Tamago means an egg; the entry gives caigo as the Cami-region equivalent. Both regional name Cami and the cited term Caigo are Japanese forms embedded in Portuguese explanation.
Tamaguiri is being startled or left astonished. The printed abbreviated principal form u is retained even though tamaguiru is the recommended full form in the preceding entry.
Tamaguqi is glossed in Latin as the male genital organ, followed by Portuguese identifying it as a decorous expression. The close-set Virgagenitalis is retained rather than silently respaced.

runs.text: Particula que ſe conjuga polla ter-

lines.note: Tamai introduces the honorific auxiliary tamau. The source describes its conjugation; the initial T, the verb conjuga, and the divided ter- correct the OCR's Famai, comcuga, and tem-.

runs.text: ceira conjugação: dà a ſuprema honra aos ver-

lines.note: Ceira completes terceira, referring to the dictionary's third conjugation. The auxiliary confers the highest honor on the verbs with which it combines; this historical classification is preserved as the source's account.

The grammatical explanation concludes, and the example begins with Deus and creation of heaven and earth. The damaged techiuo is retained provisionally rather than supplying an unestablished n or abbreviation mark for expected tenchi wo.

runs.text: Deos fez o ceo, & a terra.

lines.note: Curi completes tçu-curi, followed by honorific tamoo. The Portuguese translates God's creation of heaven and earth; the visible separation in a terra corrects the OCR's joined aterra.
Tamamatsuri denotes funeral or memorial rites. The Portuguese reads Exequias, with i rather than the OCR's e, and continues with the commemorative observance below.
The observance is performed for the deceased. Tamamatsuri wo begins an example of performing those rites, continued by suru on the following row.
Suru completes the Japanese construction and is translated as performing these funeral rites. The physical continuation remains separate from the next headword.
Tamamono is something rich or precious, or riches themselves. The two horizontal strokes at the edge form one printed hyphen, not two consecutive hyphens as in OCR.

runs.text: queza. ¶ Item, Couſa de estima, ou peça q̃

lines.note: Queza completes riqueza; a further sense is an esteemed object or gift. The relative clause explaining the gift's source continues below.

runs.text: o ſenhor deu, ou dà alguem.

lines.note: The valuable object is something a lord has given or gives to someone. The source's dà alguem is retained without supplying an additional preposition.

runs.text: Hũs bichos de varias cores, que

lines.note: Tamamushi denotes multicolored insects. The tilde abbreviation in Hũs and the historical spelling varias are retained without modernization.
The insects appear to gleam, completing the descriptive gloss for tamamushi. No unsupported species identification is added.
Tama no o is marked poetic and equated with inochi, life. The P. is upright, and the Japanese equivalent is not an embedded word within a Portuguese sentence.
Tamaki is defined as a circle or ring. The simple geometric gloss is retained without importing later specialized meanings.
Tamakiwaru is poetic and explained as life reaching its limit. The Portuguese begins morrer, to die; the P. is upright.

runs.text: rer, ou estar a vida no cabo.

lines.note: Rer completes morrer, followed by being at life's end. This is the completion of the poetic expression rather than a separate definition.
Tamari gives forms of tamaru in the sense of holding out or enduring. A- begins ame, rain, in the example of a house unable to withstand weather.

Ame and caje identify rain and wind in the description of an inadequate house. The e of caje is very faint but compatible with the surviving curve before mo; it is retained as a qualified reading, not the malformed OCR caj.

runs.text: reſiſte nem a chuua, nem ao vento. ¶

lines.note: The house resists neither rain nor wind. The worn reſiſte and chuua replace OCR Vſiſte and chaua; Miz- starts a new example continued on f469, while the separate zuga below is its catchword.
